issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For an assault trauma, the trigger pattern is difficult to reconcile clinically: explosion/bang sounds and hospital/antiseptic smells imply very different trauma contexts or aftermaths, with no accompanying memory or appraisal content linking them into a coherent assault narrative. This is more than merely unusual because the trigger set suggests mixed trauma cues rather than one assault profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'My body has been permanently damaged by what happened' does not fit well with the rest of the profile. Threat items focus on immediate environmental danger and startle, while memory items center on grief, auditory recall, and emotional numbing; none support a prominent bodily injury theme. In the absence of corroborating assault-related injury cues, this appraisal appears mismatched.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: Given the very strong Triggers → Threat edge, trigger items should plausibly feed the specific threat pattern. 'Being naked' can fit vulnerability and danger, but explosion sounds and hospital smells do not connect well to the selected threat items for a single assault formulation, making the trigger-to-threat linkage clinically incoherent.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell
issues.explanation: For an assault trauma, hospital/antiseptic smell is only coherent if the assault involved serious injury or hospital treatment, but nothing in threat, memory, or appraisals anchors the trauma to a medical context. In this profile it stands out as insufficiently connected to the rest of the formulation.

'Being naked' as a trigger implies a sexual assault, humiliation, medical exposure, or a very specific vulnerability context. The other items do not support that context: threat items reflect generalized hypervigilance/startle, memory items do not indicate bodily violation or exposure, and appraisals focus on self-blame/protection of others rather than sexualized shame. This makes the trigger hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

For an assault trauma, 'being naked' as a trigger is not impossible, but without any corroborating memory, threat, or appraisal content suggesting sexual assault, humiliation, or clothing-related vulnerability, it stands out as poorly integrated with the rest of the profile. The other trigger items point to alcohol cues and loss of control, while threat items center on hypervigilance/startle; this specific trigger appears disconnected from the described trauma representation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed
issues.explanation: 'I should have protected others and I failed' implies the patient experienced the assault in a protector/caretaker role or alongside endangered others. No memory, trigger, or threat item references other people being harmed or the patient's responsibility toward them. The rest of the appraisals are self-focused incompetence/blame, so this item is the main cross-node inconsistency.

vignette:
Samuel Okoye, a 77-year-old school principal, came to treatment at his wife’s urging after months of insisting that what happened to him “shouldn’t still have this much power.” Late one evening last year, after a school board function, he was cornered in the parking lot by a man who had clearly been drinking. The sharp smell of alcohol hit him before he fully understood what was happening. The man grabbed him, barked orders at him, and forced him toward his car while Samuel struggled to keep his footing and make sense of what he was being told to do. What stayed with him was not only the assault itself but the feeling of being overpowered by another person’s will, of having his choices stripped away in an instant. He remembers the man’s voice in fragments more than the exact words, and he has been troubled by how quickly he froze.

In the weeks afterward, ordinary moments began to feel dangerous in ways he could not dismiss. If he caught the smell of alcohol on a parent at an evening event, or on a staff member passing too closely in the hallway after a weekend, his body reacted before he could think. He would immediately look for the nearest exit, tense in his shoulders, alert to every shift around him. In those moments the old judgment returned with force: that he had failed when it mattered and that other people became dangerous without warning, ideas that felt less like thoughts than facts the reminder had just proven again. Being directed too abruptly by others could do the same; even routine situations in school, such as a district official insisting he change plans on the spot or a crowd of students pressing him along in a hallway, brought back that same sickening sense of being controlled. Those moments not only made him jumpy and reactive to movement nearby, they also pulled him back toward the assault itself. At times he could hear, in his head, the assailant’s voice as vividly as if it were beside him again.

Samuel had come to believe that the assault exposed something shameful about him. He said he should have handled it differently, should have resisted more effectively, should have known what to do. Once he was certain he could not rely on himself and that others could not be counted on either, ordinary things he would once have brushed off began to snag his attention—a sharp instruction in a meeting, a stranger standing too close, the sour trace of liquor in a hallway all started to register as potent reminders. From that grew a painful conviction that he could not rely on himself when it mattered, and, just as deeply, that other people could not be counted on either. These beliefs sharpened his sense of danger. He entered every assembly, classroom, or restaurant scanning for exits as soon as he crossed the threshold, and when someone moved unexpectedly near him he reacted as if threatened. Living in that state of alarm came to feel like its own evidence that something in him had been permanently altered, and the very fact that he was this watchful so often seemed to confirm his fear that he was no longer the steady, dependable man he had been. The more he watched for danger, the more he felt confirmed in his view that the world was unsafe and that he himself was no longer dependable.

Those same beliefs also shaped how he experienced the memory. When the event came back to him, it was often with overwhelming grief, grief not only for the assault but for the image of himself he felt he had lost. At other times he described recalling it in a strangely flat, detached way, “like it happened to somebody else,” which frightened him too; even his own memory no longer felt like something he could trust. Because he blamed himself for how he acted and no longer believed others would protect him, reminders of being forced or cornered became potent quickly. A raised voice telling him where to stand, a crowded doorway, the smell of liquor on a stranger—these were no longer minor irritants but signs that he could once again lose control.

His memory and his vigilance began feeding each other. When he noticed someone shift suddenly at the edge of his vision, he startled hard, and that jolt could bring back the sound of the attacker’s voice or a wave of grief before he even knew what had set him off. After one of these memory surges, the school around him seemed to fill with echoes of the assault; for the rest of the day he was more likely to catch on abrupt voices, crowded doorways, and any smell of alcohol as if the memory itself had taught him where to find danger. Once the memory was activated, he became even more watchful, eyes moving to doors and hands and distances between bodies. He was especially uneasy during evening school events; while greeting parents in the lobby, he kept positioning himself near exits and tracking who was entering behind him. If alcohol was on someone’s breath, the memory surged, and with it the certainty that he had failed before and might fail again.

Over time this changed both his work and his marriage. He delegated more evening responsibilities to assistant principals and avoided community receptions when he could, telling himself he was simply tired. At home, if his wife touched him unexpectedly from behind, he flinched so sharply that both of them were left shaken. He hated that reaction and took it as more evidence that he was not the steady man he had always been. Lately, even anticipating settings where he might encounter alcohol or be hemmed in by other people was enough to put him on guard before he arrived, as though the reminders were spreading outward in his mind.

What finally brought Samuel in was a recent incident at school when a student ran up beside him in the corridor and he jerked back so forcefully that the boy looked frightened. Samuel was deeply troubled by the thought that students now saw him as brittle or unsafe. He said he wants to be able to walk through his own building without searching for escape routes and without hearing that man’s voice in his head. What frightens him most is the possibility that this is who he is now: a man who cannot trust his own judgment, cannot trust other people, and can never again feel fully in command of himself.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not explicitly show reminders or triggers causing Samuel’s negative beliefs about himself or others within a single paragraph.
The vignette does not explicitly show Samuel’s negative beliefs leading him to experience more reminders or triggers within a single paragraph.
The vignette does not explicitly show the trauma memory causing reminders or triggers to arise within a single paragraph.
The vignette does not explicitly show Samuel’s sense of threat causing or intensifying his negative appraisals within a single paragraph.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not explicitly show reminders or triggers causing Samuel’s negative beliefs about himself or others within a single paragraph.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not explicitly show Samuel’s negative beliefs leading him to experience more reminders or triggers within a single paragraph.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not explicitly show the trauma memory causing reminders or triggers to arise within a single paragraph.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not explicitly show Samuel’s sense of threat causing or intensifying his negative appraisals within a single paragraph.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
